catalog_quote: In normal speech the main word stress falls on the penultimate syllable, as in Malay, with minor stress on the final syllable (Lewis 1947:18). When the penultimate syllable is a pre-syllable, this is unstressed, and the major stress falls on the last syllable. Pre-syllables do not normally have any stress and the amount of transition (i.e. its vocalic clarity, length and prominence) is conditioned by the speed and rhythm of the phrase and ranges from zero to an unstressed [ə]. ... The rule that pre-syllables do not carry stress has three exceptions, the words /demiq/ 'small', /deniya/ 'world' and /semengac/ 'spirit'. ... In tri-syllabic words there is a potential minor stress on the first syllable, when that syllable is the prefix /ber-/ /per-/ or /ter/. ... audit.recode_to: Keep the robust core (schwa pre-syllables unstressable; stress confined to the last two syllables; pre-syllable penult => final stress) but mark default primary-stress position as contested penult~final: Hogan 1988 (POP dialect) penult-main/final-minor 'as in Malay (Lewis 1947)'; Hogan 1976 (POP) even stress on both; Amon 1979 (Adang dialect, dedicated phonology) final-primary/penult-secondary, under which the record would be fixed-final rather than 'weight'. At minimum add Amon 1979 and Hogan 1976 to sources/contra with a caution line; if the catalog must pick one value, final-primary with unstressable pre-syllables is the analysis shared by the dedicated phonology and consistent with Hogan's own 'clause stress falls on the last syllable'.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding passage is verbatim in the held PL-C109 text at sec. 2.3.3, pp. 26-27 (lines 1607-1655). (2) The deciding source is a 1988 Pacific Linguistics grammar sketch + dictionary by a missionary fieldworker; its penult-stress sentence leans explicitly on a 1947 Teach Yourself Malay. (3) I fetched sources the two other open primary descriptions: Hogan's own 1976 sketch (PL C-43 p.284: stress 'falls evenly on both' minor and main syllables) and Amon Saengmani's 1979 Mahidol phonology thesis (scanned of pp.17-20, 35-37: primary stress on the final/major syllable, secondary on full-vowel minor syllables, none on pre-syllables; 'only one heavy stress... on the last syllable of disyllabic and trisyllabic words'). All three agree that reduced-vowel pre-syllables never bear stress and that prominence sits in the final two-syllable window, but they disagree on which of penult/final is

sources.citation: Saengmani, Amon. 1979. Phonology of the Urak Lawoi' language: Adang Island. M.A. thesis, Mahidol University, Bangkok. 170 pp. (sealang.net/archives/mahidol/; image-only PDF, scanned pp.17-39)
sources.quote: 'Stress in Urak Lawoi' is predictable.' Disyllables with a pre-syllable first: 'stress is on the last syllable' [be'nan]. Disyllables with a minor syllable first: 'primary stress on the last syllable and secondary stress on the first syllable' [,ka'cak], [,ma'ta] 'eye'. Trisyllables pre+minor+major: primary on last, secondary on second [se,pu'luh]; two pre-syllables + major: 'only one stress on the last syllable'; minor+minor+major: secondary on first two, primary on last [,ta,ma'ta] 'policeman'. 'it should be concluded that the words in Urak Lawoi' bear only one heavy stress, i.e. on the peak
sources.note: Only dedicated phonology of the language that is openly available; its stress-group chapter puts primary stress on the FINAL syllable (secondary on preceding full-vowel syllables), against Hogan 1988's penult-main claim on which our coding rests.

sources.citation: Hogan, David W. 1976. Urak Lawoi' (Orang Laut). In William A. Smalley (ed.), Phonemes and orthography: language planning in ten minority languages of Thailand, 283-302. Pacific Linguistics C-43. Canberra: ANU.
sources.quote: 'When both minor and main syllables occur, the stress falls evenly on both in citation form. The pre-syllable has only a vocalic transition, has no final consonant or stress, and is optional.' Minor syllable vs pre-syllable: 'The difference lies in the potential for a stress on a minor syllable'; pre-syllable transition 'ranges from zero to weak stress equivalent to the normal stress of a minor [syllable]' phrase-finally.
sources.note: Same author's earlier statement for the same (POP) dialect says stress falls 'evenly' on minor and main syllables in citation form - documents that the 1988 penult claim is an analytic choice, not a stable observation.
